about: Named places on Minjerribah / North Stradbroke Island, Quandamooka Country, Queensland. Three townships plus the wild parts. Coordinates are a single representative point per place, not a boundary. Beaches and walks are lines in the real world, so treat a beach point as somewhere on that beach rather than its exact middle.

conventions.coordinate_confidence: high = two independent sources agree within about 50 m. medium = one good public source. low = derived from a street address, a nearby feature, or a reused coordinate in the upstream data; needs a local check before anything is drawn on it.
conventions.confidence: confidence that the place exists under this name in this township, separate from how precise the coordinate is.
conventions.capacity: only present where a published number exists, or where a plain local-scale hint is genuinely useful to the simulation.

cultural_care: Quandamooka names are recorded here only where a published, citable public source uses them. Spellings vary between sources and that variation is recorded rather than resolved. No story, ceremony or site significance is invented. Where a published source states cultural significance, it is quoted narrowly and cited, and the fuller cultural record belongs in data/lore.json and docs/CULTURAL-REVIEW.md for the Traditional Owners to resolve. QYAC is the Quandamooka Yoolooburrabee Aboriginal Corporation and is the authority on all of this, not this file.

places.name: Point Lookout

alt_names.name: Mooloomba
alt_names.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Lookout_Foreshore (Queensland Heritage Register 602261 records the foreshore as also known as Mooloomba)
alt_names.note: stradbrokeisland.com spells it Mulumba; the road up to the headland is Mooloomba Road.

places.description: The ocean-side township at the island's north-east corner, and the only part of Minjerribah where the surf comes straight in off the Coral Sea. James Cook sighted and named the point from HMS Endeavour on 17 May 1770. It had 785 residents at the 2021 census, and in the summer holidays and at Easter it holds several times that, because almost every visitor bed on the island is either here or in a campground within a few minutes' drive. Everything is strung along one road: the shops and post office near Dickson Way at the western end, the pub above Home Beach, then the surf club and the gorge walk at the far eastern end.
places.best_time: June to October for whales off the headland; May to September for the cleanest surf and the least crowding.
hazards: surf and rip currents on the ocean beaches
traffic and parking pressure in school holidays

capacity.note: Peak visitor load is many times the resident population; the exact multiple is not published.

places.name: Dunwich

alt_names.name: Goompi
alt_names.note: Wikipedia records Goompi, also spelled Koompe.

places.description: The bay-side township and the island's front door. Every passenger ferry, every vehicle barge, every pallet of groceries and every ambulance transfer comes through here, which is why Dunwich feels like a working port more than a holiday town. It had 737 residents at the 2021 census and holds most of the island's services: the only school, the health service, the museum, the cemetery, QYAC's base and the barge and pontoon terminals off Junner Street. Its European history is heavy and specific: a quarantine station from 1850, then the Dunwich Benevolent Asylum from 1864 until it moved to Sandgate in 1946.
places.best_time: Any time; the town is busiest in the hour either side of a ferry arrival.
hazards: vehicle and barge traffic around the terminal
marine stingers and sharks in Moreton Bay waters

places.name: Amity Point

alt_names.name: Pulan
alt_names.source: repo-events-engine (the events engine labels the village Pulan / Amity Point throughout)
alt_names.note: Wikipedia records the name as Bulan. Both spellings are in public circulation; this needs a QYAC ruling before either is treated as settled.

places.description: The smallest of the three townships, on the island's north-west corner facing Moreton Island across the South Passage. It had 453 residents at the 2021 census. A pilot station was set up here in 1825, the first British settlement on the island, and it closed in 1848 after the paddle steamer Sovereign wrecked on the South Passage bar in 1847 with 44 dead. Amity is defined by water on three sides and by the fact that the water keeps taking the land: around 200 metres of shoreline was lost between the 1890s and the middle of the twentieth century, taking the town's racetrack and several streets with it.
places.best_time: Sunset, because it is the only township that faces west over open water. Winter for calm bay fishing.
hazards: sharks in Rainbow Channel; a fatal attack occurred in 2006
strong tidal current through the South Passage
sandflies and mosquitoes off the saltmarsh

places.name: Main Beach
places.description: The island's east-facing surf beach, running south from below the Point Lookout headland for about 33 kilometres to Jumpinpin at the far end of the island. The northern end near the surf club is where the patrol flags go up and where almost everyone swims; past that it becomes a 4WD beach and then simply empty sand. It takes the full south-easterly swell with no headland protection, so it is the biggest and most consistent surf on Minjerribah and also the most serious water.
places.best_time: Patrol hours in the warmer months for swimming. Dawn for the surf, before the north-easterly comes in.
hazards: vehicles on the sand south of the access ramp
soft sand bogging 4WDs on a rising tide

places.name: Cylinder Beach
places.description: The north-facing beach in the middle of Point Lookout, tucked behind Cylinder Headland, which is what makes it the calmest surf beach in town and the one families default to. It is patrolled in season, there is a campground directly behind it, and the walk from the beach to the shops is a couple of minutes. When the wind is a southerly and everywhere else is blown out, Cylinder is still swimmable, which is why it fills up first.
places.best_time: Mornings in a southerly. Patrol hours over summer and the school holidays.
hazards: rips form at the eastern end against the headland
crowding and parking overflow in school holidays

places.name: Home Beach
places.description: A north-facing beach at the western end of Point Lookout, looking out towards Shag Rock about 1.5 kilometres offshore. It is flatter and more sheltered than the ocean beaches further east, with the campground, the oval and the pub all sitting immediately behind it, which makes it the beach used for markets, festivals and anything that needs a crowd on sand. Adder Rock closes off its western end.
places.best_time: Late afternoon, and any time the swell is up and the east-facing beaches are unusable.
hazards: the beach carries event and camping load in peak season
places.note: The OSM point sits towards the western end near Adder Rock. Luke's events engine carries -27.427839, 153.526489 for Home Beach, about 800 m east. Both are on the beach; a mid-beach anchor should be set locally.

places.name: Deadmans Beach
places.description: A north-facing beach about 600 metres long between Cylinder Headland and the turn towards Frenchmans, with a small car park and a lookout above it. It is a short, steep walk down and there is no patrol, which keeps the numbers low even when Cylinder is packed. Good for a quiet swim on a calm day and one of the better places on the island to sit above the water and watch for turtles and rays in the clear inshore green.
places.best_time: Calm mornings. The lookout above it is good at any time.

places.name: Frenchmans Beach
places.description: An east-facing beach on the seaward side of the headland, so unlike Cylinder and Deadmans it gets no shelter at all from the prevailing south-easterly swell. Access is down a steep track. It is a surfers' and fishers' beach rather than a family one, and it is often empty on the same day the sheltered beaches are full.
places.best_time: Small clean swell and a westerly wind.

places.name: Adder Rock
places.description: The rocky headland that marks the western end of Point Lookout and the eastern end of Flinders Beach. It is the point where the long, driveable, north-facing sand of Flinders stops and the built township starts. A campground sits directly behind it on Dickson Way, and the rocks are a well-used land-based fishing spot.
places.best_time: Run-out tide for fishing off the rocks. Late afternoon for the light along Flinders.
hazards: waves washing the lower rocks on a bigger swell

places.name: Flinders Beach
places.township: between Amity Point and Point Lookout
places.description: The island's long north-facing beach, about 8 kilometres from Amity Point east to Adder Rock. It is a 4WD beach with camping permitted along the foreshore, and it faces into Moreton Bay rather than the open ocean, so the water is usually flatter than at Point Lookout. Access is by beach entry, tides matter, and a soft high tide will strand a vehicle that has misread the timing.
places.best_time: Drive it on a falling tide. Winter for camping without the heat and the mosquitoes.
hazards: getting cut off or bogged on a rising tide
dune damage if drivers leave the marked accesses

capacity.note: Minjerribah Camping states about 200 campsites on the Flinders Beach foreshore. Verify current number and permit conditions before use.

places.name: Amity Beach
places.description: The bay-side foreshore at Amity Point, backed by rock seawall in the sections that have been armoured. This is a sand-flat and tidal-channel beach rather than a surf beach: at low tide the banks run a long way out, and the deep water of Rainbow Channel comes in close near the point. It is the beach that has been retreating for over a century, and the seawall completed in 1993 is why the remaining shoreline is still there.
places.best_time: Low tide for walking the flats. Sunset for the view across to Moreton Island.
hazards: sharks in Rainbow Channel; swimming near the point is not advised

places.name: Adams Beach
places.description: A bay-facing beach about 700 metres long just south of Dunwich, looking into the southern half of Moreton Bay. It is quiet, close to the ferry, and there is a camping ground behind it. Because it is on the sheltered western side it has almost no swell, and the water is often flat enough to launch a kayak straight off the sand.
places.best_time: High tide for swimming; the flats are wide and shallow at low tide.
places.note: The coordinate is the campground point from the events engine and may sit behind rather than on the beach. The task brief paired this beach with the name Nandeebie; public sources record Nandeebie as the Quandamooka name for Cleveland on the mainland, not for Adams Beach, so no alternate name is recorded here. See DATA-NOTES.

places.name: Bradbury's Beach
places.description: A small bay-side beach between the Dunwich ferry terminal and One Mile, with a camping ground on the foreshore. It is the closest camping to the ferry, which makes it the arrival-side option for people who do not want to drive further, and it sits right on the water with the anchored boats of the One Mile anchorage just to the north.
places.best_time: High tide. Early morning for the working boats going out.

places.name: Point Lookout headland

alt_names.name: Mooloomba
alt_names.source: Queensland Heritage Register 602261, Point Lookout Foreshore, also known as Mooloomba
alt_names.note: Listed on the Queensland Heritage Register on 27 August 2004 as a state heritage landscape.

places.description: The rhyolite headland at the island's north-east corner, and the reason the town exists where it does. It is high, cliffed, and cut by steep narrow gorges with rock shelves and inlets at the bottom of them, and it carries the whole eastern approach to the island. The heritage listing covers the foreshore including Frenchmans, Deadmans and Cylinder beaches, the two gorges, Whale Rock, Cylinder Headland and Camel Rock. Standing on it in winter you can see humpbacks passing close enough to hear them blow.
places.best_time: June to October for whale migration. Early morning for the light on the water and before the car park fills.
hazards: the rock shelves below are washed by sets and should not be walked on a rising swell

places.name: North Gorge
places.description: A narrow inlet cut into the north side of the headland where the swell funnels in, hits the back wall and blows straight up. It is the single most-watched piece of water on the island: from the boardwalk above it people see turtles, manta rays, dolphins and, in season, whales inside a few hundred metres of the cliff. The gorge is a viewing place rather than a swimming place; there is no safe way down into it.
places.best_time: A moderate swell for the surge in the gorge. June to October for whales. Early morning for light and quiet.
hazards: crowding on the boardwalk in peak season

places.name: South Gorge
places.description: A pocket beach of about 200 metres of sand at the bottom of the headland's southern side, reached by stairs from the end of Kennedy Drive with street parking up on Mooloomba Road. It is sheltered from the northerlies and the water inshore is calmer than Main Beach, which is exactly why people underestimate it. It is not patrolled and there is a persistent rip working out along the rocks.
places.best_time: Northerly wind days when Cylinder and Deadmans are choppy.
hazards: stair access only, hard with gear or small children

places.name: North Gorge Walk
places.description: The boardwalk and clifftop loop around the headland, roughly 1 to 1.5 kilometres, with two entrances off Mooloomba Road about 150 metres apart depending on whether you want to start on the north or south side. It is a mix of dirt track, boardwalk and intermittent stairs, and it is the thing almost every visitor to the island does at least once. The Redland City Council project extending the clifftop route is called the Minjerribah Panorama Coastal Walk. There is a bus stop on the island route named Point Lookout Gorge Walk, so it is reachable without a car.
places.best_time: First light or last light. Whale season, June to October, for the reason most people come.
hazards: parking overflow onto Mooloomba Road in peak season

places.name: Whale Rock
places.description: A rock formation with a blowhole on the Point Lookout headland, named in the Queensland Heritage Register citation for the Point Lookout Foreshore alongside Cylinder Headland and Camel Rock. It sits on the seaward side of the gorge walk, and the blowhole works when the swell is big enough and coming from the right direction.
places.best_time: Big south-easterly swell, when the blowhole is working.
hazards: wave wash on the lower rocks
places.note: The name and the blowhole are confirmed by the heritage citation, but no gazetteer or OSM coordinate was found. The lat and lon here are an estimate placed on the seaward side of the gorge walk and must be corrected locally.

places.name: Cylinder Headland lookout
places.description: The low headland between Cylinder Beach and Deadmans Beach, with a picnic and barbecue area on top and views both ways along the north coast. It is the shelter that makes Cylinder Beach calm, and it is the everyday lookout, the one locals stop at rather than the one on the tourist route. Named in the Point Lookout Foreshore heritage listing.
places.best_time: Late afternoon. Winter for whale spotting without walking the full gorge track.

places.name: Point Lookout Lighthouse
places.description: A small navigation light on Lucinda Crescent above the headland, constructed in 1932. It is not a visitor attraction and it is not the tall coastal tower people expect from the name, but it is a fixed reference point on the highest built part of the town and it marks the corner of the island for shipping standing off the South Passage.
places.best_time: Not a destination; visible in passing.
hazards: private and residential surrounds; no public access to the structure

places.name: Blue Lake

alt_names.name: Karboora
alt_names.note: stradbrokeisland.com spells it Kaboora and gives the meaning as deep silent pool. Both spellings are in public use.

places.township: inland, Naree Budjong Djara National Park
places.description: A window lake in the middle of the island: not a perched lake sitting on a clay pan, but a place where the sand has been cut down far enough to expose the water table, so the lake is the groundwater itself showing through. It is about 7.3 hectares and 9.4 metres at its deepest, its overflow drains into Eighteen Mile Swamp, and sediment work has shown it has been remarkably stable for thousands of years. Reaching it is a walk of roughly 5.2 kilometres return through wallum woodland, stunted eucalypt, wallum banksia and heath. It is a place of special cultural significance to Quandamooka people.
places.best_time: Early morning, before the heat. Cooler months for the walk.
hazards: no shade on much of the track
no drinking water on the track
the lake is a protected and culturally significant place; check current park conditions and access rules before going
places.note: Access rules and any cultural conditions change. Check Queensland Parks and QYAC before treating this as open.

places.name: Brown Lake

alt_names.name: Bummiera
alt_names.note: Wikipedia records Bummeria as an alternative spelling.

places.township: inland, about 4 km east of Dunwich
places.description: A perched lake about 4 kilometres east of Dunwich on Brown Lake Drive, sitting above the water table on a sealed organic pan rather than draining into it. The water is the colour of strong tea because tea tree and other vegetation leach tannins into it, making it an acidic, dystrophic system with very little in it that eats. There is a park with picnic and toilet facilities at the northern edge. Published sources record it as a women's place of deep significance to Quandamooka people, and in 2020 the first all-women QYAC and Queensland Parks ranger team carried out a planned cultural burn there.
places.best_time: Mid-morning on a still day, when the surface goes glassy.
hazards: culturally significant place; follow QYAC and Queensland Parks guidance on use, and do not assume swimming is appropriate
places.note: The cultural material here is summarised from published sources only. The fuller record and any protocol belongs in data/lore.json and docs/CULTURAL-REVIEW.md for QYAC to resolve.

places.name: Naree Budjong Djara National Park

alt_names.name: Naree Budjong Djara
alt_names.note: Published translation: My Mother Earth. The park absorbed the former Blue Lake National Park.

places.description: The national park covering a large part of the island's interior, declared in 2011 and jointly managed by the Quandamooka Yoolooburrabee Aboriginal Corporation and Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service. It takes in Blue Lake and the former Blue Lake National Park, and the country in it is wallum heath, stunted eucalypt woodland and swamp rather than rainforest. Joint management is the practical point: this is a park where the Traditional Owners are a management partner, not a consulted party.
places.best_time: April to October, for walking without the heat.
hazards: closures for cultural burns and park works
places.note: The coordinate is a centroid over a very large area and does not represent any usable point. Use the Blue Lake coordinate for anything the player interacts with.

places.name: Myora Springs

alt_names.name: Capembah
alt_names.source: https://stradbrokeisland.com/myora-springs/ (spelled Capeembah) and the OSM waterway named Capembah Creek
alt_names.note: Spelling varies between sources: Capembah and Capeembah both appear.

places.township: between Dunwich and Amity Point, on East Coast Road
places.description: Freshwater springs on the bay side of East Coast Road a few kilometres north of Dunwich, where clear water rises out of the sand and runs through the mangroves into Moreton Bay. There are large shell middens of cockle, oyster and whelk near the creek mouth. A short walkway lets you see the springs without walking on the ground. Dogs are not allowed in the area. It is also one of the few places the false water rat has been recorded, a rare nocturnal native rediscovered here in 1978 after being thought gone.
places.best_time: Any time; it is a short stop rather than a walk. Cooler and quieter early.
hazards: middens are a protected cultural site; stay on the walkway
places.note: The coordinate is the Myora Conservation Park centroid from OSM. A separate OSM node named Myora Springs sits about 1.2 km inland at -27.4687, 153.4254, which does not match a spring that runs into the bay. The roadside boardwalk point needs a local fix. Moongalba, the sitting-down place associated with Oodgeroo Noonuccal, is nearby but is a separate place and is not recorded here.

places.name: Dunwich ferry terminal, Junner Street pontoon
places.description: The passenger pontoon on Junner Street where the SeaLink water taxi from Toondah Harbour at Cleveland lands. It is the single busiest square hundred metres on the island: the bus route meets the boat here, the taxis wait here, and the arrival and departure rhythm of the whole island is set by this pontoon and the barge ramp beside it. The crossing takes about 45 to 60 minutes on the SeaLink boats.
places.best_time: Avoid the hour either side of a long-weekend departure.
hazards: vehicle and pedestrian conflict at the terminal
queueing onto Junner Street and Ballow Road

places.name: Dunwich barge ramp
places.description: The vehicle ferry ramp in the Dunwich terminal precinct, where the barges from Toondah Harbour land cars, trucks, freight and the island's groceries. Everything on wheels that is on Minjerribah arrived up this ramp. Barge loading order, tide and weather set what does and does not reach the island on a given day, which is why a rough easterly on the bay shows up two days later as a gap on a shop shelf.
places.best_time: Not a visitor destination. Watch it if you want to understand island logistics.
hazards: queue backing onto the road on long weekends
places.note: The ramp exists and is in this precinct, but public data did not let me separate the barge apron from the passenger pontoon. The coordinate is the terminal precinct and needs a local fix. Stradbroke Ferries' ticket office is at -27.5032366, 153.4015771 per OSM; the White Pages listing gives a Ballow Road address, which suggests the ramp is a short way south of the pontoon.

places.name: One Mile Jetty
places.description: The jetty on Yabby Street at the One Mile anchorage, about a kilometre north of the main Dunwich terminal, where the Stradbroke Flyer water taxi lands. The crossing from Cleveland takes about 30 minutes, which is why people in a hurry use this one. The anchorage in front of it holds the island's moored boats and is the flattest sheltered water on this side.
places.best_time: Any Flyer departure. Evening for the anchorage and the light off the bay.

places.name: Polka Point
places.description: The small point on the Dunwich foreshore north of the ferry terminal, with a picnic and barbecue area on it. It looks straight west over Moreton Bay towards the mainland, which makes it the sunset spot for the Dunwich side and a standing fixture in local film location lists. Quiet, close to town, and the water in front of it is shallow and tidal.
places.best_time: Sunset. Low tide for the flats.

places.name: Amity Point boat ramp
places.description: The public boat ramp at Amity Point, and the main launching point for anyone fishing the South Passage, Rainbow Channel or the Amity banks. It is the closest ramp on the island to the northern bay grounds, so it carries far more traffic than the size of the village suggests, particularly on a fine winter weekend. The current through the channel here is strong and launching and retrieving on a running tide takes care.
places.best_time: Slack water either side of the tide change. Winter for calm bay conditions.
hazards: trailer congestion and parking overflow on weekends
places.note: The events engine carries -27.4010812, 153.4388024 for the ramp, about 125 m east of the fishing club KMZ value used here. The two may be the ramp and the jetty park respectively.

places.name: Amity Point jetty
places.description: The public jetty at Amity Point, off Claytons Road with a park beside it. It is a fishing and looking jetty rather than a ferry jetty: nothing scheduled lands here. It sits on the shoreline that has been retreating for over a century, so the ground around it is the actively managed part of the erosion problem, with rock seawall on either side.
places.best_time: Run-out tide for fishing. Sunset for the view to Moreton Island.
hazards: shoreline slumping in the surrounding foreshore
places.note: No gazetteer or OSM record was found for the jetty structure. The coordinate is the Amity Point Jetty Park point from the events engine and will be on land rather than on the jetty.

places.name: Amity Point erosion and slump zone
places.description: The stretch of Amity Point foreshore, on the seaward side of Ballow Street, where the bank periodically slumps into Rainbow Channel. The mechanism is a flow slide rather than ordinary wave erosion: saturated sand fails and drops away, sometimes taking metres of land in one event, driven by the eastward migration of the deep channel against the shore. Survey records show the foreshore retreating since 1886. Redland City Council runs a Shoreline Erosion Management Plan for it, a geotechnical hazard zone is assessed and buildings and infrastructure are moved out of it, and the University of Queensland has run research into the flow slide events.
places.best_time: Not a destination. Relevant to the simulation as a slow, occasionally sudden, land-loss process.
hazards: deep water and strong current immediately offshore
places.note: The coordinate is an approximate mid-point of the affected reach west of Ballow Street and is not a surveyed boundary. The council SEMP documents divide the shoreline into northern and central reaches; use those for anything precise. The task brief called this a sand blow; the published mechanism is foreshore slumping and flow slides, which is a different thing from a wind-driven sand blow.

places.name: Little Ship Club
places.description: The licensed club and waterfront bistro on Yabby Street at One Mile, overlooking the anchorage. It is the main social venue on the Dunwich side, running a bistro, a game fishing club and a calendar of community events, and it is one of the small number of places on the island where a large mixed crowd reliably shows up in the same room.
places.best_time: Evenings and weekends. Watch the club calendar for its annual events.
hazards: licensed venue; transport home is limited after the last bus

places.name: Point Lookout Surf Life Saving Club
places.description: The surf club at 24 Kennedy Drive, sitting at the northern end of Main Beach where the flags go up. It is the coastal safety hub for the ocean side of the island and it also functions as a club venue and a gathering point for beach events. Everything about swimming safety at Point Lookout runs from here, on the only stretch of the 33 kilometre Main Beach that is patrolled at all.
places.best_time: Patrol hours in the warmer months. Nippers and club events on weekends in season.
hazards: the beach in front is only patrolled between the flags and only in patrol hours

places.name: Point Lookout Bowls Club
places.description: The bowls club at the western end of Point Lookout near Dickson Way, doing far more than bowls: club meals, functions, and a standing meeting point for local groups. The Point Lookout Fishing Club uses it as its meeting and briefing venue. On an island with very few indoor rooms that hold a crowd, a club like this carries a share of civic life that its size does not suggest.
places.best_time: Club nights and weekends.
hazards: licensed venue; limited transport home after the last bus

places.name: North Stradbroke Island Historical Museum
places.description: The island museum at 15 to 17 Welsby Street, Dunwich, established in 1987 and run across four buildings. It holds an Aboriginal room, a pioneer room, lighthouse and shipping displays, a whale skull on loan from the Queensland Museum, and an archive of local documents and images. It is the anchor for the Goompi Dunwich heritage walk and it is where most locally held documentary evidence about the asylum, the quarantine station and the shipwrecks actually lives.
places.best_time: Check opening hours before travelling; it is volunteer-supported and not open every day.

places.name: Dunwich Cemetery
places.description: One of the earliest surviving cemeteries in Queensland, on Bingle Road, covering about 3.3 hectares and holding an estimated 10,000 burials. The first is believed to date from 1847, a victim of the wreck of the Sovereign. It holds the dead of the 1850 typhus outbreak from the Emigrant, including the doctors who treated them, and 8,426 former inmates of the Dunwich Benevolent Asylum buried between 1867 and 1947. It closed to new burials in 1952. Most asylum graves are unmarked; a memorial wall built from the bricks of the old asylum laundry carries nameplates that are added as identifications are confirmed. Many of those buried are believed to be descendants of the Traditional Owners.
places.best_time: Any daylight hours. It is a working place of remembrance for island families, not a tourist site.
hazards: treat as a place of respect

places.name: Dunwich Benevolent Asylum site
places.description: The site of the institution that shaped Dunwich for eighty years. A quarantine station operated here from 1850 to 1864, where 26 people died in the 1850 typhus outbreak. It was converted to the Dunwich Benevolent Asylum in 1864, one of Queensland's first such facilities, taking in the aged, the destitute and the chronically ill from across the colony, and it ran until it moved to Sandgate in 1946. At its peak the asylum population was larger than the town around it, and its records are one of the most substantial nineteenth century social datasets in Queensland.
places.best_time: Approach it through the museum, which holds the archive and runs the heritage walk.
hazards: remnant structures and ruins; check what is publicly accessible before treating any part as open
places.note: The coordinate is an estimate in the Dunwich township and is not a surveyed site boundary. Asylum remains are dispersed and partly on land in other uses. Needs a local fix and a check of what is publicly accessible.

places.name: Amity Point Community Club
places.description: The community club at Amity Point, running meals, meetings and local social events. In a village of a few hundred people it is the room that everything happens in, and it is one of the very few indoor spaces on the western side of the island that will hold a whole-of-village gathering.
places.best_time: Club opening hours; check before travelling.

places.name: Point Lookout Community Hall and library
places.description: The community hall on Dickson Way, which also houses the Redland City Council public library branch for Point Lookout. It carries concerts, workshops, talks, meetings and the wet-weather fallback for anything planned outdoors, which on an ocean-facing headland is a role that gets used.
places.best_time: Library hours and event nights.

places.name: Dunwich State School
places.description: The only school on Minjerribah, at 37 Bingle Road, Dunwich, opened in 1904. It takes students from all three townships, which means children from Point Lookout and Amity Point ride the island bus each day, and it means the school run is one of the fixed daily flows across the whole island rather than a local one. It runs a special education program alongside its mainstream classes.
places.best_time: Term time, weekday mornings and afternoons for the bus and traffic pattern.
hazards: school zone traffic on Bingle Road
bus movements at start and end of day

places.name: Dunwich swimming pool and sports precinct
places.description: The island's swimming pool and its adjoining sports area, at the Dunwich school precinct on Bingle Road. On an island ringed by water this is still the only place to swim without a rip, a shark or a stinger, which makes it where children learn to swim and where heat-safe activity goes in summer.
places.best_time: Summer, and check current opening arrangements before travelling.
hazards: supervision and opening hours vary; confirm before relying on it
places.note: The events engine coordinate for the pool is identical to the OSM coordinate for Dunwich State School, so the pool is either on or immediately beside the school grounds. Worth a local confirmation of whether it is a school facility, a council facility, or shared.

places.name: Ron Stark Oval
places.description: The main sports oval at Dunwich, and the island's biggest flat piece of usable public ground. The North Stradbroke Island Rugby League and Allsports Club sits in the corner of it. It carries community sport, carnivals, markets, food vendors and fireworks, and it is the default answer whenever an event needs more space than a hall.
places.best_time: Weekend sport in season. Community event days.
hazards: no shade over most of the ground
vehicle access across turf during events

places.name: Point Lookout Oval
places.description: The oval behind Home Beach at Point Lookout, bookable through Redland City Council. It carries music, markets, surf events and spectator crowds as much as it carries sport, because it is the only large open space on the ocean side of the island that sits directly behind a beach.
places.best_time: Event weekends and school holidays.
hazards: parking overflow onto surrounding streets during events
no shade over most of the ground

places.name: Bob Jarrett Park
places.description: A park named in the task brief that could not be confirmed from any public source. It does not appear on the Redland City Council or stradbrokeisland.com park lists, which between them name Headland Park, Cylinder Beach Park, Point Lookout Hall Park, Adder Rock Park, Amity Point Jetty Park, Old School House Park, Junner Street Park, Petrie Street Park, Dunwich Foreshore Fitness Park, the two Dunwich skate parks, Amity Point Skate Park and Brown Lake Park. It is very likely a locally used name for a place that is signed differently, or a facility not listed online.
places.note: Deliberately left with null coordinates rather than a guess. Needs Luke to say which park this is and which township it is in, then it gets a real record.

places.name: Headland Park
places.description: The park on Mooloomba Road at the top of the headland, with picnic and barbecue facilities, toilets, and the Captain Cook memorial marking the 1770 naming of the point. It is the staging ground for the gorge walk: most people park here, walk the loop and come back to it. The seat of knowledge and the Look Cafe picnic tables sit in the same precinct.
places.best_time: Early or late; the car park fills through the middle of the day in season.
hazards: cliff edges beyond the park boundary

places.name: Cylinder Beach Park
places.description: The park on East Coast Road behind Cylinder Beach, with picnic and barbecue facilities and toilets. It is the service edge of the busiest family beach on the island, so on a hot school holiday afternoon the barbecues and the toilet block here carry more people than most of the island's venues.
places.best_time: Weekday afternoons if you want a barbecue without waiting.

places.name: Amity Point Jetty Park
places.description: The foreshore park on Claytons Road beside the Amity Point jetty and boat ramp, with picnic and barbecue facilities, toilets and a skate park. It is the village's public front room: the place people wait, eat, launch, land and watch the channel from.
places.best_time: Sunset. Weekend mornings during the boat launch rush.

places.name: Dunwich Foreshore
places.description: The foreshore park strip on Cunningham Street beside the ferry terminal, with a playground, an enclosed swimming enclosure for children, picnic and barbecue shelters, toilets, a fitness park and a skate park. It is the first thing a visitor sees stepping off the boat, and it is also where island families spend an ordinary Saturday, which is an unusual combination and worth preserving in the simulation.
places.best_time: High tide for the swimming enclosure. Any afternoon for the playground.

places.name: Brown Lake Park
places.description: The day-use area on Brown Lake Drive at the edge of Brown Lake, with picnic and barbecue facilities and toilets. It is the only serviced stop between Dunwich and the inland tracks, and it is the point where the visitor load on a culturally significant lake is concentrated and managed.
places.best_time: Mornings. Cooler months.
hazards: cultural sensitivity of the lake itself; follow QYAC and Queensland Parks guidance

places.name: Adder Rock campground
places.description: The camping ground on Dickson Way behind Adder Rock at the western end of Point Lookout, operated by Minjerribah Camping. It is the largest of the Point Lookout grounds and takes tents, campervans, caravans and cabins, so it carries a lot of the peak visitor load that the township itself cannot house.
places.best_time: Outside school holidays if you want a site without booking months ahead.

capacity.note: Published site counts; confirm current numbers with Minjerribah Camping.

places.name: Cylinder Beach campground
places.description: The camping ground directly behind Cylinder Beach, taking glamping, caravans and tents. It is the most in-demand ground on the island because it puts you on the calmest patrolled beach with the shops a short walk away, and it books out for Christmas and Easter well in advance.
places.best_time: Shoulder season. Peak periods require booking far ahead.
hazards: density and noise in peak season
no vehicle access to the beach from here

places.name: Home Beach campground
places.description: The camping ground behind Home Beach, taking caravans and tents, operated by Minjerribah Camping. It sits between the oval and the beach on the sheltered north-facing side of Point Lookout, which is why it is the ground that events and festivals lean on.
places.best_time: Shoulder season. Event weekends fill it.
places.note: The events engine reuses this exact coordinate for several different Dickson Way facilities, so it is a precinct point rather than a campground entrance. Needs a local fix.

places.name: Thankful Rest
places.description: A camping area adjacent to Home Beach at Point Lookout, historically opened only during peak periods. It does not appear on the current Minjerribah Camping campground list, and at least one travel source states that the old Thankful Rest campground is now called Home Beach campground. The name is still in local use whether or not it is still a separate booking.
hazards: status uncertain; do not plan around it without confirming
places.note: Deliberately left with null coordinates. Two readings are possible: a still-operating peak-period overflow area beside Home Beach, or a historical name now absorbed into Home Beach campground. Luke will know which. See DATA-NOTES.

places.name: Amity Point campground
places.description: The camping ground on the Amity Point foreshore, taking glamping, caravans, cabins and tents. It is the fishing ground: people bring boats, launch at the ramp a short walk away and work the channel. It is also the sunset side of the island, which is the other reason people book it.
places.best_time: Winter for calm bay fishing and no mosquitoes.
hazards: mosquitoes and sandflies off the saltmarsh in the warmer months

places.name: Flinders Beach camping area
places.description: Foreshore beach camping along Flinders Beach, 4WD access only, with about 200 sites spread along the sand rather than in a formed ground. There are no powered sites and facilities are minimal; the appeal is that you camp on the beach and drive on and off it. Tide timing decides whether you can get in or out.
places.best_time: Falling tide for access. Winter for camping without heat and mosquitoes.
hazards: getting cut off or bogged by the tide
vehicles on the sand near camps
no facilities; carry water and take rubbish out

capacity.note: Published figure from Minjerribah Camping; confirm current permit conditions.

places.name: Main Beach camping area
places.description: Beach camping along the east-facing Main Beach south of Point Lookout, 4WD access only. It is the exposed side of the island: full swell, full sun, no shelter and no facilities. Camping here is a self-sufficient exercise, and it is the closest most people get to the island's long empty eastern shore.
places.best_time: Falling tide for access. Cooler months.
hazards: getting cut off or bogged by the tide
no facilities; carry water and take rubbish out
places.note: The coordinate sits near the northern access at Point Lookout rather than along the camping stretch, which runs many kilometres south.

places.name: Bradbury's Beach campground
places.description: The camping ground on Bradbury's Beach between the Dunwich ferry terminal and One Mile, taking glamping, caravans and tents. It is the arrival-side option: close enough to the ferry to walk, on flat sheltered bay water, and the ground people use when they want to be near the boats rather than near the surf.
places.best_time: Any time; quieter than the Point Lookout grounds.

places.name: Adams Beach campground
places.description: The camping ground behind Adams Beach just south of Dunwich, taking caravans and tents. It is the quietest of the serviced grounds, on the bay side, close to the ferry and away from the visitor concentration at Point Lookout.
places.best_time: Any time; rarely under the pressure the Point Lookout grounds carry.
